```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

# Load the real Kaggle Olympic dataset (271,116 rows and 15 columns)
olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define a consistent group of 12 major European Olympic countries (including Spain)
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", # Spain
  "GBR", # Great Britain
  "FRA", # France
  "GER", # Germany
  "ITA", # Italy
  "SWE", # Sweden
  "NOR", # Norway
  "NED", # Netherlands
  "HUN", # Hungary
  "FIN", # Finland
  "SUI", # Switzerland
  "POL"  # Poland
)

# Count only one medal per unique event and country so team sports are not overcounted
medals_unique <- olympics |>
  filter(!is.na(Medal)) |> # Keep only medal-winning entries
  distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal) # Deduplicate team medals
```

## Introduction

::: {.dashboard-card}
I decided to study the Olympics because I really like sports and I am interested in comparing the United States with European countries. I want to see who has won more medals, which sports different countries are best at, and how Olympic results have changed over time. I also want to focus a little more on Spain because I am from there.

This project builds on my Milestone 2 work using the [**120 Years of Olympic History: Athletes and Results**](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/heesoo37/120-years-of-olympic-history-athletes-and-results) dataset from Kaggle. The dataset contains **271,116 rows and 15 columns**, covering both Summer and Winter Olympic Games from **1896 to 2016**. Because the dataset ends in **2016**, more recent Olympic Games (such as Tokyo 2020 or Paris 2024) are not included in this analysis.
:::

## Variables Used in This Project

::: {.dashboard-card}
To explore Olympic performance across countries and over time, I use the following key variables from the dataset:

- **`Year`**: to see how Olympic results and medal counts change over time from 1896 to 2016.
- **`NOC` and `Team`**: to identify countries using their official National Olympic Committee (`NOC`) 3-letter codes and team names.
- **`Sport` and `Event`**: to compare different sports (like Swimming, Athletics, and Sailing) and individual medal events.
- **`Medal`**: to count `Gold`, `Silver`, and `Bronze` medals won.
- **`Sex`**: to explore differences in participation and medal counts between male (`M`) and female (`F`) athletes.
- **`Age`**: to explore athletes' ages across regions and sports.

```{r}
#| label: age-sex-summary

# Quick summary of athlete age and sex among medalists in the USA and our 12 European countries
olympics |>
  filter(!is.na(Medal), NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |> # Keep medalists in our study group
  mutate(Region = if_else(NOC == "USA", "United States", "Selected Europe (12 Countries)")) |> # Group into USA vs Europe
  group_by(Region, Sex) |>
  summarise(
    Medalist_Rows = n(), # Number of medal-winning athlete rows
    Average_Age = round(mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE), 1), # Mean age of medalists
    Median_Age = median(Age, na.rm = TRUE), # Median age of medalists
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Region", "Sex", "Medalist Athlete Entries", "Average Age", "Median Age"),
    caption = "Athlete Age and Sex Overview for Medalists (1896–2016)"
  )
```
:::

## Methodology: Counting Medals Fairly & Defining Europe

::: {.dashboard-card}
Two important choices make our comparison accurate and fair:

1. **Counting unique event medals instead of athlete rows:** In the raw dataset, every player on a winning basketball, soccer, or rowing team gets their own row. If we simply counted rows, a single basketball gold medal would count as 12 medals! To avoid overcounting team sports, I use `distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal)` so that each country receives **one medal per event**.
2. **Consistent European Selection (12 Countries):** Throughout all charts, I use a clearly defined set of 12 European Olympic countries: **Spain (`ESP`), Great Britain (`GBR`), France (`FRA`), Germany (`GER`), Italy (`ITA`), Sweden (`SWE`), Norway (`NOR`), Netherlands (`NED`), Hungary (`HUN`), Finland (`FIN`), Switzerland (`SUI`), and Poland (`POL`)**.

::: {.note-callout}
**Why Group vs. Individual Comparisons Matter:** Comparing the **United States (`2,823` medals)** against **12 European countries combined (`6,849` medals)** is very different from comparing individual countries. In the Olympics, each European nation sends its own full delegation of athletes and teams, so combining 12 countries naturally produces a larger group total. However, when we compare **individual countries one-on-one**, the United States (`2,823` medals) has won nearly three times as many medals as the highest-ranking European country in our group, Germany (`1,004`), followed by Great Britain (`919`) and France (`879`).
:::
:::

## 1. USA vs. Europe: Olympic Medals Over Time (1896–2016)

::: {.dashboard-card}
This first interactive chart tracks total unique event medals won in each Olympic year from **1896 to 2016** (combining Summer and Winter Games held in the same year). You can hover over any point to see the exact year and medal total.

Notice how the 12 European countries combined usually win more medals as a group, while the United States alone reaches massive peaks (such as 1904 in St. Louis and 1984 in Los Angeles) and competes closely with an entire continent's worth of teams.

```{r}
#| label: chart-1-medals-over-time
#| fig-height: 5.5

# Count unique event medals by Year for the USA vs. the 12 selected European countries
medals_by_year <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |> # Keep USA and selected European NOCs
  mutate(
    Group = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries Combined)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(Year, Group, name = "Medals") # Count unique medals per year and group

# Create the ggplot2 time-series line chart
p1 <- ggplot(medals_by_year, aes(x = Year, y = Medals, color = Group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + # Draw trend lines over time
  geom_point(size = 2.3) + # Highlight each Olympic year
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries Combined)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1896, 2016, by = 16)) +
  labs(
    title = "USA vs. Selected European Countries: Unique Event Medals Over Time",
    subtitle = "Combined Summer & Winter Olympic medals per Olympic year (1896–2016)",
    x = "Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

# Convert to an interactive Plotly chart
ggplotly(p1, tooltip = c("x", "y", "colour")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )
```
:::

## 2. Top Olympic Sports: USA vs. Selected European Countries

::: {.dashboard-card}
Which sports drive these medal totals? The chart below shows the **top 10 medal-winning sports** across the USA and our 12 selected European countries from 1896 to 2016.

Even when compared against 12 European countries combined, the **United States actually leads in Swimming (`550` vs. `411`)** and is nearly tied in **Athletics (`816` vs. `822`)**! Meanwhile, the selected European nations have a large collective advantage in **Fencing (`424` vs. `32`)**, **Cycling (`423` vs. `57`)**, **Canoeing (`329` vs. `16`)**, and **Rowing (`314` vs. `89`)**.

```{r}
#| label: chart-2-top-sports
#| fig-height: 6

# Find the top 10 sports overall by unique event medals among USA + 12 European countries
top_10_sports <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  count(Sport, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  pull(Sport)

# Count medals by Sport and Region for those top 10 sports
sports_comparison <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs), Sport %in% top_10_sports) |>
  mutate(
    Group = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(Sport, Group, name = "Medals") |>
  mutate(Sport = fct_reorder(Sport, Medals, .fun = sum)) # Order sports by total medals

# Build horizontal grouped bar chart
p2 <- ggplot(sports_comparison, aes(x = Sport, y = Medals, fill = Group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.72) + # Side-by-side bars for USA vs Europe
  coord_flip() + # Flip axes so sport names are easy to read
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#ec4899",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. 12 European Countries (1896–2016)",
    subtitle = "Unique event medals won in the most contested Olympic sports",
    x = "Olympic Sport",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    fill = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p2, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )
```
:::

## 3. Focus on Spain: Olympic Medal History (1900–2016)

::: {.dashboard-card}
Because I am from Spain (`ESP`), I wanted to take a closer look at how Spain's Olympic performance has evolved over time. Through 2016, Spain has won **150 unique event medals** (**45 Gold**, **63 Silver**, and **42 Bronze**), with its top sports being **Sailing (19 medals)**, **Canoeing (16)**, **Cycling (15)**, **Athletics (14)**, and **Tennis (12)**.

As the chart below clearly shows, **1992 was the turning point in Spanish Olympic history**. When Barcelona hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics, Spain invested heavily in athlete training and won **23 total medals in 1992** (22 in Summer—including 13 Golds—and 1 Bronze in Winter). Since 1992, Spain has remained a strong Olympic contender at every Summer Games through 2016.

```{r}
#| label: chart-3-spain-history
#| fig-height: 5.5

# Filter unique medals for Spain (ESP) and order Medal factor levels
spain_medals <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC == "ESP") |> # Keep only Spain
  mutate(Medal = factor(Medal, levels = c("Gold", "Silver", "Bronze"))) |> # Order Gold, Silver, Bronze
  count(Year, Medal, name = "Medals") # Count Spain's medals per Olympic year and type

# Create a stacked bar chart of Spain's medals over time
p3 <- ggplot(spain_medals, aes(x = Year, y = Medals, fill = Medal)) +
  geom_col(width = 2.8) + # Stacked bars for each Olympic year Spain won a medal
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Gold" = "#fbbf24",   # Gold accent
      "Silver" = "#cbd5e1", # Crisp silver
      "Bronze" = "#ec4899"  # Vibrant pink accent for Bronze
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2016, by = 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Spain's Olympic Medal History by Medal Type (1900–2016)",
    subtitle = "Notice the dramatic breakthrough at the 1992 Barcelona Games (23 total medals)",
    x = "Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won by Spain",
    fill = "Medal Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p3, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.25, y = 1.12)
  )
```
:::

## Conclusion & Data Source

::: {.dashboard-card}
Looking at 120 years of Olympic data from **1896 to 2016**, the answer to *"Who dominates the Olympics?"* depends on how we frame the comparison:

- **As a group of 12 countries**, our selected European nations have won more combined unique event medals (`6,849`) than the United States (`2,823`), largely because 12 separate countries can enter many more athletes and teams across every sport, especially in Cycling, Fencing, Canoeing, and Rowing.
- **As a single country**, the **United States** is by far the most dominant individual nation in Olympic history, winning nearly triple the medals of any single European country and even beating all 12 European countries combined in Swimming.
- **Spain (`ESP`)** transformed its Olympic program starting with the **1992 Barcelona Olympics**, growing from winning only a few medals per Games before 1992 to consistently winning between 11 and 20 medals at every Summer Olympics through 2016.

**Original Dataset:** [120 Years of Olympic History: Athletes and Results (Kaggle)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/heesoo37/120-years-of-olympic-history-athletes-and-results)
:::
